title: How a Liquidity Pool Really Works
objectives: Understand the constant-product formula x · y = k
Discover why pool depth directly determines price impact
Test low vs high liquidity with identical trade sizes
Avoid the beginner trap of trading into thin pools

steps.title: The Shared Piggy Bank
steps.body:
In traditional stock markets, buyers wait for sellers in an order book: if nobody wants to sell exactly when you want to buy, you simply cannot trade. DeFi threw that model in the bin. Instead, you trade against a shared <Term id="liquidity_pool">liquidity pool</Term> run by an <Term id="amm">AMM</Term> (Automated Market Maker) - a robot shopkeeper with no order book and no waiting around.

**The shared piggy bank analogy.**

Picture a public piggy bank holding two tokens: **SOL** and **fUSDC**. Anyone can walk up, drop in SOL, and take out fUSDC. No human sets the price - one formula does it:

`x · y = k`

- `x` = the amount of SOL sitting in the vault.
- `y` = the amount of fUSDC sitting in the vault.
- `k` = their product, a number the pool is forbidden from changing. Every trade must leave `x · y` exactly the same.

Because `k` can never change, the pool can never run out of a token and can always quote a price for any trade size. The price is simply the ratio of the two reserves: if the vault holds 10 SOL and 2,000 fUSDC, one SOL is worth 200 fUSDC.

**Why you should care about depth.**

The *size* of the vault (its <Term id="tvl">TVL</Term>) decides how much your own trade moves the price. Drop $50 into a $4,000 pool and you feel it immediately. Drop $50 into a $400,000 pool and it is a rounding error. That effect is called <Term id="price_impact">price impact</Term>, and it is the number-one hidden tax on careless traders.

In this lesson you will trade the exact same size against a tiny pool and an ocean-deep pool, and watch price impact collapse from scary to invisible. Buckle up.

steps.title: The Liquidity Lab

goal.description: Switch between Shallow and Deep pools with a 50 fUSDC trade to see price impact drop from over 2.4% to under 0.05%!

hints: Select the 'Deep Pool' toggle on the right.
Observe how the price impact readout immediately shrinks toward zero.
Use the trade slider to experiment with trade sizes up to 500 fUSDC.

steps.title: What Just Happened? Price Impact
steps.body:
The exact same 50 fUSDC trade produced two completely different outcomes. Here is the breakdown:

- **Shallow Pool ($4,000 TVL):** your 50 fUSDC was a big fraction of the vault, so it dragged the price several percent against you. That self-inflicted price move is <Term id="price_impact">price impact</Term>.
- **Deep Ocean Pool ($400,000 TVL):** the same 50 fUSDC was a drop in the ocean, so the price barely twitched and you received far more SOL.

Why should you care? Price impact is the silent loss you never see on a trade confirmation. It is what turns a 'great entry' into a mediocre one, and it combines with <Term id="slippage">slippage</Term> to decide whether your trade actually fills at the price you saw.

**Rule of thumb: deeper pools give safer, fairer trades.** When in doubt, check the pool's depth before you size up - and always split monster orders across pools or use an aggregator.

steps.title: Under the Hood: Deriving x · y = k
steps.body:
Why does x · y = k behave this way? 

Let a pool hold 100 SOL (x) and 10,000 USDC (y). The product k is 100 × 10,000 = 1,000,000. 
When a trader puts in 10 SOL, the new SOL reserve becomes 110. To keep k = 1,000,000, the new USDC reserve must become 1,000,000 / 110 = 9,090.91 USDC. 

The trader receives 10,000 - 9,090.91 = 909.09 USDC (giving an effective price of $90.91/SOL instead of the initial spot price of $100/SOL).
That 9.09% drop is price impact! Because x is in the denominator, larger trades relative to pool depth experience exponentially worse pricing.

questions.prompt: What does 'k' represent in the constant product formula x · y = k?
options: The daily transaction volume of the exchange
The invariant product of the two token reserves, which AMM smart contracts preserve across every swap
The network gas fee paid to Solana validators
The total number of users who have joined the pool
questions.explainRight: Correct! 'k' is the constant product (x × y) that the pool's formula forces to stay the same on every swap. That single constraint is what makes the pool able to price any trade without ever running out of tokens.
questions.explainWrong: Not quite. 'k' is the invariant product of the two reserves (reserveA × reserveB). Because a swap must keep x · y equal to k, the pool can always find a new price that keeps the product constant.

questions.prompt: Why can't traders simply drain a pool of all its SOL in one giant buy?
options: Because as the SOL reserve shrinks, each remaining SOL becomes more expensive, so buying the last coins becomes unattractive
Because AMM pools hard-lock withdrawals after 10 trades in a day
Because Solana validators block any transaction larger than 1% of pool reserves
Because the pool automatically re-mints SOL the moment reserves get low
questions.explainRight: Exactly! The constant product k puts the reserve in the denominator: as SOL leaves the pool, the price of each remaining SOL climbs steeply. The market prices your demand into the curve, and the last fraction of a pool is essentially priceless.
questions.explainWrong: Not that. The protection is built into the math: the x · y = k formula means a shrinking SOL reserve drives the price of SOL up exponentially, pricing out further purchases long before the pool is empty.

questions.prompt: You want to swap a large amount of tokens with the least possible price impact. What should you look for?
options: A pool with the highest fee tier
A pool created less than a minute ago
A pool with high Total Value Locked (deep liquidity)
A pool with only 1 holder
questions.explainRight: Correct! TVL is the size of the vault, and a deep pool absorbs your order as a tiny fraction of reserves. That keeps price impact close to zero instead of pricing your own trade against you.
questions.explainWrong: No. The fund that matters is reserve size (TVL). A big order in a tall pool is a small wave; the same order in a puddle pool is a tsunami that drags the price against you.

questions.prompt: A pool holds 100 SOL and 10,000 USDC. A trader swaps in 10 SOL. Roughly how much USDC do they receive?
questions.explainRight: Correct! New SOL reserve = 110, and to keep k = 1,000,000, the USDC reserve must become 1,000,000 / 110 ≈ 9,091, so the trader receives 10,000 − 9,091 ≈ $909. The effective price works out to ~$90.91/SOL versus the $100 spot price - that gap is price impact.
questions.explainWrong: Close, but do the math: with 10 SOL added, reserves become 110 SOL and x · y must stay 1,000,000, so the USDC side drops to ~9,091. The trader takes out the difference: about $909, not a straight 10 × 100.

questions.prompt: After you buy SOL from an AMM, why does the next SOL you buy cost slightly more?
options: The pool re-prices every hour using yesterday's trades
Buying SOL shrinks the SOL reserve, so each remaining SOL is scarcer and the curve prices it higher
The pool charges a hidden surcharge on repeat buyers
Validators impose a memory tax on frequent traders
questions.explainRight: Exactly. With x · y = k, reducing x (SOL) forces y to rise to keep the product constant, which means the price of SOL in USDC goes up. Every buy makes the next one pricier - that's the AMM's built-in supply and demand.
questions.explainWrong: No. There's no surcharge or tax - it's pure scarcity math. Each purchase reduces the SOL reserve, and the constant-product formula converts that shortage directly into a higher SOL price for the next buyer.

questions.prompt: Which statement about price impact is TRUE?
options: Price impact only matters for trades under $10
All pools produce identical price impact for the same trade size
Deep pools magnify price impact
Price impact shrinks as pool reserves grow, but grows non-linearly as your trade size approaches the full reserve
questions.explainRight: Correct. Price impact is a ratio: your trade over the pool reserves. Bigger reserves = smaller ratio = less impact, and because x sits in the denominator, impact explodes worse-than-linearly as trades approach the reserve size. That non-linearity is the hidden tax on careless traders.
questions.explainWrong: Not quite. Price impact is relative: it depends on your trade size compared to pool reserves. Because of the x in the denominator, it snowballs non-linearly as your trade approaches the reserve, and always gets smaller as the pool gets deeper.

questions.prompt: You swap the same 50 USDC in two pools: Pool A has $4,000 TVL and Pool B has $400,000 TVL. Which statement is TRUE?
options: Pool B returns noticeably more SOL for the same 50 USDC
Both pools return identical SOL because the trade size is the same
Pool A returns more SOL because it needs the volume
Deep pools reject trades under $100
questions.explainRight: Correct. In Pool A your $50 is ~1.25% of the vault, dragging the price several percent against you; in Pool B it's a rounding error. Same input, different output - the shallow pool quietly eats your money as price impact.
questions.explainWrong: No. Trade size is identical, but price impact is not - it depends on trade size relative to reserves. In the shallow pool your trade is a meaningful chunk of the vault, so you receive meaningfully less SOL for the same 50 USDC.
